frontMatter.introduction: Each SOP in this manual applies to the relevant site(s) as specified in its scope section. All procedures have been developed to ensure consistent, safe, and compliant execution of tasks – from incoming raw material inspection and solar cell/module production to quality assurance, warehousing, maintenance, and customer support – in alignment with national and international standards (including ALMM, BIS, IEC, and UL requirements).
frontMatter.objective:
The primary objectives of this SOP Manual are:
Standardisation: To establish a uniform method for executing each critical process, minimising variability and human error.
Quality Assurance: To uphold Gautam Solar’s commitment to high-efficiency Mono PERC and N-Type TOPCon modules, ensuring every panel meets our rigorous performance and durability benchmarks (e.g., low degradation, >90% power output after 20 years).
Safety & Compliance: To protect employees, equipment, and the environment by embedding safety protocols and regulatory requirements into every procedure.
Training & Onboarding: To serve as the primary training resource for new and existing employees, enabling them to understand and follow approved methods.
Continuous Improvement: To provide a baseline for audits, performance monitoring, and future revisions as technology and regulations evolve.
frontMatter.scope:
This manual applies to all employees, contractors, and temporary workers engaged in activities that affect product quality, safety, or operational efficiency at any of the above three Gautam Solar locations. The SOPs cover, but are not limited to, the following functional areas:
Incoming quality control (raw materials, cells, glass, encapsulants)
Manufacturing operations (cutting, stringing, lamination, framing, junction box attachment)
In-process and final testing (EL testing, IV flash testing, dielectric withstand, thermal cycling)
Warehouse and inventory management
Preventive and corrective maintenance of automated production lines
Health, safety, and environmental (HSE) procedures
Non-conformance handling and corrective action (CAPA)
Customer complaint resolution
Administrative processes at the Registered Office (e.g., procurement, HR, documentation)
The manual does not replace statutory or regulatory documents but complements them by translating external requirements into actionable internal steps.
frontMatter.reviewMechanism:
To establish a single, standardised, and centralised process for reviewing, amending, approving, and continuously improving all Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) within the Gautam Solar SOP Manual. This mechanism replaces any individual review sections that were previously embedded within individual SOPs and ensures:
Uniform governance across all SOPs.
Consistent application of document control (aligned with GS-DC-001).
Clear assignment of review responsibilities.
Retrospective effectiveness checks on a manual-wide basis.
Traceable revision history and approval records.

This central review mechanism applies to every SOP in the Gautam Solar SOP Manual, regardless of department (Quality, Production, HSE, Product Development, Compliance, IT, etc.) or site (Delhi, Haridwar, Bhiwani). It covers:
Scheduled periodic reviews.
Triggered reviews (due to incidents, regulatory changes, process changes).
Amendment procedures (minor and major revisions).
Approval and distribution of revised SOPs.
Retrospective effectiveness assessment of changes.

Role responsibilities: General Manager – overall owner of the review mechanism, ensures reviews are conducted on time, maintains the master review schedule, approves all final changes. Process Owner (Department Head) – initiates review for SOPs within their department, coordinates input from subject matter experts, submits proposed changes to the Document Controller. Document Controller – assigns review tracking numbers, maintains the review log, distributes draft revisions, collects feedback, and archives obsolete versions. Internal Audit – provides independent assessment of review effectiveness during periodic audits (see GS-AUD-001). All SOP Users (Employees) – may propose improvements at any time via the SOP Improvement Request form (GS-DC-F03).
Note: The General Manager assumes the approval authority previously held by the QA Manager. For day-to-day coordination, the QA Manager (or a designated Quality lead) may support the process, but final sign-off rests with the General Manager.

Scheduled periodic reviews: Every SOP shall be reviewed according to a risk-based schedule maintained by the General Manager (with support from the Document Controller). Default intervals: High-risk / frequently used – Annually (e.g., GS-QC-001 IQC, GS-PR-001 Production Startup/Shutdown, GS-WM-002 Water & Heavy Metals). Medium-risk – Every 2 years (e.g., GS-EN-001 Energy Efficiency, GS-WM-001 Waste Management). Low-risk / stable – Every 3 years (e.g., GS-DC-001 Document Control – except its own review must be done every 2 years). The General Manager may adjust intervals based on audit findings or regulatory changes.
Triggered reviews (ad hoc): An off-schedule review shall be initiated within 30 days of a regulatory change affecting the SOP’s legal basis, a major incident where the SOP failed to prevent or mitigate it, a significant process change, a recurring non-conformance (more than two similar findings in 12 months), or a user-initiated improvement request validated by the Process Owner.

Review process steps: 5.1 Initiation – the Process Owner (or General Manager) creates a Review Initiation Record containing SOP number and title, reason for review, proposed changes (or a statement “no changes required after assessment”), and proposed reviewers (minimum 2, including at least one user of the SOP). 5.2 Assessment & Drafting – the Process Owner with reviewers examines the SOP against current operations, regulations and best practices; if changes are needed a draft revision is prepared using the standard SOP template; if not, the “no change” decision is recorded and the next review date recalculated. 5.3 Consultation & Feedback – the draft is circulated electronically to relevant department heads and affected employees (minimum 5 working days for comment); comments are collated by the Document Controller and substantial disagreements resolved through a review meeting chaired by the General Manager. 5.4 Approval – the final draft goes to the General Manager; changes affecting regulatory compliance or introducing new safety-critical steps also require the HSE Manager and, if applicable, the Compliance Officer; version numbers are assigned per GS-DC-001 (major = +1.0, minor = +0.1). 5.5 Distribution & Training – the Document Controller replaces the master copy in the ERP and marks the previous version “SUPERSEDED”; printed copies are recalled and replaced; training on the revised SOP is arranged via GS-DC-F06 and must be completed before the new version becomes effective. 5.6 Retrospective Effectiveness Check – for every major revision, a check is conducted six months after the effective date by Internal Audit or an independent reviewer, answering: have the intended improvements been achieved; have unintended side effects appeared; is the revised SOP being followed as trained. Results are documented in GS-REV-RETRO-01 and presented to the General Manager; persistent issues trigger a new triggered review.

Central Review Log & Annual Summary: all review activities are recorded in the Central Review Log (GS-REV-LOG-01) with fields for Review ID, SOP number, review trigger, initiation date, reviewers, changes made, approval date, retrospective check due date and completion status. The General Manager shall produce an Annual Review Summary Report by 31 January each year for the Audit Committee and CEO.

Emergency amendments: where an immediate correction is required to address an imminent safety, environmental or legal risk, the General Manager may authorise an emergency amendment documented on GS-REV-EMERG-01; it becomes effective immediately but must be followed by a full review, including retrospective check, within 30 days, and is reversed if the full review does not confirm it.

Relationship with Document Control (GS-DC-001): this mechanism operates within GS-DC-001 for numbering, storage, approval signatures and training acknowledgement. Individual SOPs no longer contain their own Revision History or Review Procedure sections beyond a simple reference to the Review ID from the Central Review Log and the date.

Records: GS-REV-LOG-01 Central Review Log (10 years, Document Controller); GS-REV-RETRO-01 Retrospective Effectiveness Report (5 years after closure, Internal Audit); GS-REV-EMERG-01 Emergency Amendment Record (10 years, General Manager); GS-DC-F03 SOP Improvement Request Form (3 years, Process Owner). All records stored in \\GautamSolar\QA\Central_Review\.

References: GS-DC-001 – Document Control & SOP Management (version 1.0 or later); GS-AUD-001 – Internal Audit & Monitoring; ISO 9001:2015 – Clause 7.5 and Clause 9.3.

This Central Review Mechanism is effective from the date of final approval. All SOPs in the manual shall be subject to this mechanism. Any printed copy of this mechanism is uncontrolled after 24 hours.

sops.title: Incoming Quality Control (IQC) for Raw Materials

blocks.text: The purpose of this SOP is to define a standardised procedure for inspecting, testing, and accepting or rejecting all incoming raw materials used in the manufacturing of solar modules at Gautam Solar. This ensures that only materials meeting defined quality specifications enter production, thereby preventing defects, reducing rework, and maintaining the high performance and reliability of our Mono PERC and N-Type TOPCon modules.
This SOP applies to all raw materials received at Gautam Solar's factory locations, including but not limited to:

Solar cells (Mono PERC, N-Type TOPCon)
Tempered glass (front and rear)
Encapsulants (EVA, POE)
Backsheet
Frames (aluminium)
Junction boxes (with diodes)
Ribbons (interconnector, busbar)
Potting compound
Sealants / adhesives
Packaging materials (pallets, corrugated boxes, stretch film)
Applicable locations:

Factory Unit 1, Plot 67-70, Sec-8A, SIDCUL, Haridwar, Uttarakhand – 249403
Factory Unit 2, 7 KM Milestone, Tosham Road, Bhiwani, Haryana – 127032
This SOP does not cover consumables (e.g., cleaning cloths, gloves) or office supplies, which are handled by storekeeping under a separate procedure.

responsibilities: Performs visual, dimensional, and functional inspections as per this SOP; records results; issues NCRs for non-conformances.
Notifies QA of new receipts; segregates quarantine area; manages physical movement of accepted/rejected materials.
Communicates with suppliers regarding rejections and corrective actions.
Reviews non-conformance reports; decides on material disposition (rework, accept under concession, return); approves supplier CAPAs.
May be consulted for urgent material decisions; uses only QA-approved materials.

blocks.text:
IQC Checklist for each material type (see Section 8 – Appendix A for examples).
Approved supplier list with material specifications.
Sampling plan table (based on AQL 0.65 for critical defects, 1.0 for major, 2.5 for minor – see Appendix B).
Calibrated instruments: Vernier calliper, micrometer, thickness gauge, EL tester (for cells), IV flash tester (for sample cells), glass strength tester (if available), multimeter (for junction boxes).
NCR (Non-Conformance Report) forms (GS-QC-F01).
Quarantine area clearly marked with red tape or signs.
IQC log (electronic or paper).

rows: Supplier delivery arrives. Store Supervisor verifies basic paperwork (challan, packing list).
Store Supervisor notifies QA department of new receipt via daily receipt log or direct intimation.
QA Inspector locates the material in the quarantine holding area (physical receipt pending inspection).
Identify the lot size (number of pieces, rolls, pallets).
Refer to Sampling Plan (Appendix B) to determine the sample size (e.g., for cells: ANSI/ASQ Z1.4, General Inspection Level II).
Randomly select samples from different packages/pallets to represent the entire lot.

body.text:
Visual check: No damage, cracks, stains, discoloration, foreign particles, deformation.
Dimensional check: Measure key dimensions against approved drawing/specification sheet.
Packaging integrity: No moisture ingress, torn bags, crushed corners.
If any of this fail, proceed to Section 5.6 (Non-Conformance Handling).
A. Solar Cells (Mono PERC / TOPCon)

rows: No edge chips >0.5 mm, no microcracks visible, no broken corners, no finger interruption
No dark areas, cracks, or broken fingers; uniform brightness
Power (Pmax) within ±3% of datasheet; Voc, Isc, FF within spec

body.text: B. Tempered Glass (Front & Rear)

rows: No scratches >0.1 mm width; no bubbles >1 mm; no edge chips >2 mm length
3.2 mm ± 0.2 mm (or as per product spec)

body.text: C. Encapsulants (EVA / POE)

rows: No gel spots, foreign particles, wrinkles, or uneven colour
Gel content ≥75% for EVA (per supplier certificate)

body.text: Note: Full cross-linking verification is performed during production lamination trials; IQC accepts based on supplier batch certificate + random visual.
D. Backsheet

rows: No wrinkles, pinholes, delamination, or contamination
>40 N/cm (if tester available; otherwise rely on supplier cert)

body.text: E. Aluminium Frame

rows: No dents, scratches, anodising defects, burrs

body.text: F. Junction Box (with Diodes)

rows: No cracks, missing gasket, terminal deformation
Gasket properly seated (full IP test only on sample to certified spec)

body.text: G. Ribbons (Interconnector / Busbar)

rows: Would cause immediate product failure or safety hazard (e.g., broken cell, glass chip exposing sharp edge, diode short circuit).
Affects performance or durability (e.g., low cell efficiency, glass warpage > spec, EVA thickness out of spec).
Reject or accept under concession with QA Manager approval.
Cosmetic or slight dimensional deviation not affecting performance (e.g., small scratch on frame, minor edge chip < spec).
Accept with notification to supplier. May be logged for trend analysis.

body.text: Sampling decision rule (AQL based):

Number of defective samples ≤ Acceptable limit → ACCEPT the lot.
Number of defective samples ≥ Reject limit → REJECT the lot.
Refer to Appendix B for AQL tables.

If all criteria are met, QA Inspector stamps or labels each package with "IQC APPROVED" (green sticker) and signs the inspection report.
Material is moved from quarantine to the store accepted area.
QA Inspector updates the IQC Log (GS-QC-F02) with lot number, date, supplier, result, and batch release number.
Store Supervisor issues material to production only when approved.

QA Inspector documents all failures on the Non-Conformance Report (NCR) – Form GS-QC-F01.
Material is marked "REJECTED – HOLD" (red sticker) and moved to quarantine rejection zone.
QA Manager reviews the NCR and decides:

Return to supplier (full rejection) – Purchase department issues debit note / return request.
Rework at supplier cost (e.g., cleaning, repackaging) – only if feasible.
Accept under concession (for minor/major defects that do not impact final product safety or warranty) – Production and QA Manager sign off.

For concession acceptance, a Concession Tag (GS-QC-F03) is attached to the lot specifying the deviation and authorising use.
Supplier is notified and a Corrective Action Request (CAR) may be issued for recurring issues.
QA retains a copy of the NCR in the monthly quality file.
If production requires immediate release of material before full IQC is completed:

Stop-gap procedure: QA performs a quick "critical attributes" inspection (visual only) and marks as "RELEASED UNDER PROTEST" with a time-limited tag (max 48 hours).
The full IQC must be completed within 48 hours. If final inspection fails, production is stopped, and any WIP using that material is segregated and re-evaluated.
Such cases require prior approval of QA Manager and Production Head.

rows.retention: Attached to lot until consumption; then filed for 1 year

The purpose of this SOP is to establish a standardised, safe, and efficient procedure for starting up and shutting down the solar module production lines at Gautam Solar. Proper startup ensures that all equipment is ready for operation, quality parameters are met from the first module, and safety hazards are avoided. Proper shutdown prevents equipment damage, saves energy, and leaves the line in a safe state for the next shift or maintenance.
This SOP applies to all automated and semi-automated production equipment used in the manufacturing of Mono PERC and N-Type TOPCon solar modules, including but not limited to:

Stringer machines (cell tabbing and stringing)
Layup station (glass, EVA, cell matrix, backsheet)
Laminator (curing and encapsulation)
Framing press / automatic framing line
Junction box attachment and soldering station
Curing oven (for silicone / potting compound)
Flash tester (IV measurement)
EL tester (electroluminescence imaging)
Hi-Pot tester (dielectric withstand)
Conveyor systems and turn tables

responsibilities: Ensures startup and shutdown procedures are followed by line operators; authorises line start after pre-start checks; signs shift handover log.
Performs the startup and shutdown steps as described; records any deviations or abnormalities.
Responds to equipment faults discovered during startup; performs scheduled warm-up and calibration as needed.
Verifies first-module quality after startup (first-off inspection); may halt line if quality fails.
Approves emergency or unplanned shutdowns; coordinates with Maintenance and QA.

blocks.text:
Operator training: All operators must be trained on this SOP and on the specific equipment they operate (training records maintained by HR/Production).
Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): Safety glasses, cut-resistant gloves, safety shoes, and ear protection (where noise >85 dBA).
Checklists: Pre-startup checklist for each major equipment type (see Appendix A).
Shift log book or digital log (e.g., ERP or Excel) to record startup/shutdown times, issues, and handover notes.
Compressed air, power, and cooling water must be available and within specified ranges (checked by Maintenance before shift).
Material availability: Raw materials (cells, glass, EVA, backsheet, ribbons, frames) must be staged and IQC-approved.

rows: Arrive 10 minutes before shift start. Put on required PPE.
Check shift handover log from previous shift for any known issues, ongoing maintenance, or material deviations.
Visually inspect the line: No tools left on equipment, no loose wires, guards in place, emergency stops not pressed.
Verify utilities: Check that compressed air pressure is 6–7 bar, main power is on, cooling water flow present (where applicable).
Perform pre-startup checklist for each machine (see Appendix A – sample).
Turn on the main control panel for each machine. Wait for HMI (touch screen) to boot.
Home or reference all axes (for stringers, pick-and-place robots). Follow machine-specific homing procedure.
Load consumables: Ribbon spools, flux, solder wire, EVA rolls, backsheet rolls as per machine instructions.
Run a dry cycle (without cells / glass) for stringers and laminator to warm up heaters and stabilise temperature.
Set process parameters on HMI: temperature profiles (stringer soldering iron, laminator zones), vacuum levels, conveyor speeds. Verify against standard recipe for the product being run.
Perform a sample run with 5–10 cells or 1 mini-laminate.
Send sample to QA for first-off inspection (EL, IV, visual).
Wait for QA approval before starting full production. If QA rejects, troubleshoot and repeat step 11–12.
Record startup completion in shift log (time, parameters, any issues).
Begin normal production at rated speed.

steps.heading: A. After Scheduled Maintenance or Breakdown

body.text:
Maintenance Technician must sign off that equipment is ready for operation (using GS-MT-F01 – Maintenance Completion Form).
Perform an extended warm-up (30 minutes) and a full qualification run of 10 consecutive good modules before releasing the line.
QA must approve first 3 modules.

steps.heading: B. Monday Morning / After Long Shutdown (>48 hours)

body.text: In addition to the standard startup, perform a full cleaning of:

Laminator silicone blanket and chamber
Stringer nozzles and flux applicator
Conveyor belts

Run a dry cycle for 30 minutes minimum.
Calibrate temperature controllers using a reference thermometer.

steps.heading: C. After Material Change (e.g., different cell size or ribbon type)

body.text:
Load new material.
Perform a trial run of 5 modules.
QA to inspect all 5 before resuming full production.

steps.heading: Standard Daily Shutdown (End of Shift / End of Production)

rows: Stop feeding new materials into the line. Allow all WIP (work-in-progress) to complete the process.
Run out all modules from laminator, framing, curing oven, and testing stations. Do not leave partially processed units inside equipment.
For laminator: Set to “idle” or “cool down” mode. Do not turn off immediately – allow temperature to drop naturally to <80°C before full shutdown to avoid blanket damage.
For stringers: Turn off heater cartridges first. Wait 5 minutes, then turn off the main power.
For curing oven: Turn off heating elements but leave exhaust fan running for 10 minutes to remove residual fumes.
Remove and clean any adhesive residue, flux residue, or glass fragments from the line.
Return unused consumables to proper storage (ribbon rolls, flux bottles, etc.).
Shut down the main control panel for each machine (follow reverse order of startup).
Disconnect compressed air at the machine level (if required by machine manual).
Perform end-of-shift housekeeping: Sweep around machines, empty scrap bins, clean work surfaces.
Record end-of-shift data in log: total modules produced, downtime minutes, any abnormal events.
Complete shift handover log for the next shift, noting any pending issues or maintenance needs.
Ensure all emergency stops are NOT activated (they should be in normal position for next shift).
Turn off lights and lock the control panel if required by site safety rules.

body.text: An emergency shutdown is performed when there is an immediate safety risk, fire, smoke, or major equipment failure.

rows: Press the nearest emergency stop (E-stop) button – red mushroom button. This will immediately cut power to moving parts.
Do not attempt to restart until the hazard is eliminated.
Evacuate the area if there is fire, electrical arcing, or chemical spill.
Call for help: Security / Fire brigade (if needed) and Production Supervisor.
After emergency is resolved, only Maintenance and Supervisor may reset E-stops and perform a controlled restart using the “After Breakdown” procedure (Section 5.2 A).

body.text: Important: Do not use emergency shutdown as a normal shutdown method – it can damage equipment (e.g., laminator blanket left at high temperature without cooling).
On Fridays (or last shift of the week), in addition to daily shutdown:

Drain any water-cooled systems (if freezing risk in winter).
Clean all adhesive nozzles and replace with storage fluid per machine manual.
Cover sensitive optical equipment (EL cameras, vision systems) with dust covers.
Turn off main compressed air supply to the entire line at the header.
Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) for any equipment that will undergo maintenance over the weekend.
Log all actions in the maintenance log and shift log.

This SOP provides a comprehensive, actionable framework for Gautam Solar to:

Systematically reduce energy intensity (kWh per solar module produced) through procurement, operation, and retrofitting of energy-efficient equipment. The goal is a measurable year-on-year decline in absolute energy consumption and specific energy use.
Implement waste heat recovery and cogeneration (CHP) to capture thermal energy that would otherwise be lost to the environment, converting it into useful heating or additional power. The system must continuously generate at least two distinct forms of energy (e.g., electricity + hot water / steam) from a single fuel source.
Minimise emissions of fluorinated greenhouse gases (F-gases) – which have high Global Warming Potential (GWP), often thousands of times that of CO₂ – by improving operational design, conducting proactive leak detection and repair, and responsibly decommissioning old equipment.
Reduce energy consumption of IT infrastructure (data centres, server rooms, networking, UPS, desktops) without compromising reliability or performance. This includes optimising cooling, virtualisation, storage, and end-user power management.
Each section includes technical explanations, calculation methods, example targets, and reporting protocols to ensure consistent application across all Gautam Solar sites.
The SOP applies to all energy-carrying systems and emission sources at all three locations:

rows: Electric motors (all sizes), air compressors, HVAC (heating, ventilation, air conditioning), lighting (indoor, outdoor, street), production machinery (stringers, laminators, curing ovens, testers), pumps, fans, office equipment
Emergency/standby generators (covered under separate contingency SOP)

Laminator exhaust gases, cooling water from stringer soldering stations, compressor intercooler and aftercooler heat, CHP engine/generator unit (if installed), furnace/oven flue gases, any thermal fluid systems
Heat below 40°C where recovery is uneconomical (justified in feasibility study)

Split ACs, VRV/VRF systems, window ACs, packaged units, chillers, cold storage (canteen), refrigerated air dryers, SF₆-insulated switchgear, laboratory refrigerators, vehicle ACs (excluded – handled by transport SOP)
Small hermetically sealed units (<1 kg charge) – still inventoried but leak checks less frequent

On-premises servers (physical and virtual), network switches/routers/firewalls, storage arrays (SAN, NAS), server room cooling (CRAC/CRAH, in-row coolers), UPS for IT, desktop PCs, laptops, monitors, printers, scanners, data centre lighting
Cloud services (energy accounted by provider but choice of region/efficiency considered)

steps.heading: 4.1 Energy-Efficient Equipment – Reducing Energy Intensity Over Time

body.text: 4.1.1 Why Energy Intensity Matters

Energy intensity (kWh per module) decouples energy use from production volume. Even if production grows, intensity can fall, meaning each module costs less energy to make. Gautam Solar targets 5% annual reduction in intensity for the first five years, resulting in a cumulative 20–25% improvement by Year 5.
Example calculation:
If intensity rises >5% from previous month, investigate root causes: degraded equipment, improper settings, new inefficient machine, or measurement error.
4.1.2 Procurement Minimum Efficiency Standards
Electric Motors (all new and replacement):

Standard: IE3 (Premium Efficiency) for 0.75–375 kW (IEC 60034-30).
For motors running >4,000 hours/year (most production motors), IE4 (Super Premium Efficiency) is recommended based on lifecycle cost analysis.
Do not purchase: IE1 (Standard) or IE2 (High) except for very intermittent duty (<500 hrs/year) with documented approval.
Air Compressors (screw type):

Must have Variable Speed Drive (VSD) if flow demand varies by >20% (typical in factories with shift operations).
Minimum efficiency: ISO 50001 Class 2 or better.
For fixed speed compressors, require a load/unload controller and adequate receiver tank sizing (>200 litres per 100 cfm).
Lighting:

All new and replacement luminaires: LED only.
Luminous efficacy ≥100 lumens/W for indoor high bay (factory), ≥120 lumens/W for linear tubes.
For outdoor floodlighting: ≥130 lumens/W with correlated colour temperature (CCT) ≤4000K (better visibility and less glare).
Install daylight sensors near windows and occupancy sensors in warehouses, corridors, and toilets.
HVAC (Air Conditioners, Chillers):

Split and packaged ACs: Minimum 5-star BEE rating (India) or ISEER ≥4.5.
Chillers (if >20 kW): Screw or centrifugal type with VSD. Minimum IPLV (Integrated Part Load Value) ≥0.70 kW/ton for water-cooled, ≥1.0 kW/ton for air-cooled.
Production Machinery (Stringers, Laminators, Ovens):

Request Specific Energy Consumption (SEC) from supplier in kWh per unit output (e.g., kWh per 1,000 strings or kWh per module laminated).
Compare SEC with current equipment baseline. Target ≥15% reduction for any replacement.
4.1.3 Sub-metering & Data Collection
Install Class 1.0 accuracy digital energy meters at the following points:
Data recording frequency:

Daily: All meters (by shift supervisor).
Weekly: Calculate energy intensity using production pieces from shift log.
Monthly: Energy Manager compiles into energy dashboard.
4.1.4 Energy-Efficient Operation Guidelines
For air compressors (often 10–20% of factory electricity):

Set discharge pressure to minimum required (typically 6.5 bar instead of 7.5 bar). Every 1 bar reduction saves 7–10% energy.
Fix all air leaks (audit monthly using ultrasonic detector).
Install zero-loss condensate drains instead of timer drains.
Reduce inlet air temperature (duct outside air if cooler than compressor room).
For laminators:

Verify insulation integrity – infrared scan for hot spots.
Do not keep laminator idle at full temperature for >30 minutes; use standby mode (lower platen temperature) if break is longer.
Optimise cycle time – adjust vacuum and pressure ramp rates per supplier manual.
For lighting:

Clean luminaires every 6 months (dust reduces output by 20–30%).
Replace T8 fluorescent with LED tube lights (saving 50–60%).
Implement zone control – turn off lights near windows during daytime.
4.1.5 Retrofit & Replacement Plan
Annually (Q4), Energy Manager prepares a Capital Energy Retrofit Plan listing:

Equipment with highest energy intensity (bottom 10%).
Estimated savings (kWh/year), cost, payback.
Prioritisation: payback <2 years → immediate; 2–4 years → include in next year's budget; >4 years → evaluate if combined with other upgrades.
Example table snippet:
4.2.1 Principles & Technical Background

Waste heat is thermal energy generated as a by-product of industrial processes (laminators, compressors, ovens) that is normally rejected to the atmosphere via cooling water or exhaust air. Waste heat recovery (WHR) captures a portion of this heat and uses it for space heating, pre-heating process inputs, or generating additional power.

Cogeneration (Combined Heat and Power – CHP) takes this further: a single prime mover (gas engine, gas turbine, steam turbine, or biomass gasifier) simultaneously produces electricity and usable heat. Typical total efficiency reaches 80–90% compared to ~35–45% for grid electricity alone.
Why this applies to Gautam Solar:

Laminators operate at 140–160°C; their cooling water and exhaust contain significant heat.
Air compressors produce 80–90°C hot air from the oil cooler and aftercooler.
If a CHP unit is installed, it can run on natural gas or biomass (available in Haridwar/Bhiwani areas) and provide both on-site power and hot water for pre-heating laminator platens or cleaning.
4.2.2 System Configuration (Conceptual – adapt to actual installed equipment)
Option A – Standalone Waste Heat Recovery (no CHP yet):

rows: Pre-heat boiler feedwater, washing water for glass
Generate low-pressure steam or hot water
Pre-heat water for canteen or cleaning

body.text: Option B – CHP Unit (Natural Gas Engine or Biomass Gasifier)

rows: Burns natural gas to rotate generator – produces electricity.
Recovers heat from engine jacket water (90°C) and exhaust gas (500°C) via heat exchangers.
Hot water at 80–90°C or low-pressure steam – supplied to laminator pre-heating, factory space heating, or an absorption chiller (for summer cooling).

body.text:
Key performance indicator: Total Efficiency = (Electrical output + Thermal output) / (Fuel input energy content, in same units).
Target: ≥80% (e.g., 35% electrical + 50% thermal = 85%).
4.2.3 Feasibility & Installation Steps
Before implementing WHR or CHP, a feasibility study must be conducted:

Identify all waste heat streams (temperature, flow rate, duration per shift, yearly hours).
Calculate recoverable energy using formula:
Q = ṁ × Cp × ΔT
– ṁ = mass flow rate (kg/s)
– Cp = specific heat (kJ/kg·K) – for water ~4.18, air ~1.005
– ΔT = temperature drop across heat exchanger (K)
Determine thermal demand (how much hot water / air is actually needed).
Economic analysis: Installed cost, annual savings (fuel/electricity avoided), payback period. Aim for payback ≤4 years.
Obtain environmental clearance if CHP unit exceeds threshold (consult state pollution control board).
After feasibility approval, follow this SOP for Operation & Maintenance (Section 4.2.4).
4.2.4 Operation Procedure – Waste Heat Recovery (Non-CHP)

rows: Check heat exchanger cleanliness – differential temperature across HX. If ΔT is >5°C below design, schedule cleaning.
Monitor bypass valves – ensure they are not unintentionally diverting flow away from recovery.
Log temperatures – Inlet and outlet on hot side, inlet and outlet on cold side. Calculate recovered energy (kWh) using flow meter readings.
For ducted compressor heat: Adjust dampers to send heated air to warehouse in winter (damper open) and exhaust outside in summer (damper closed).

body.text: Recovered energy calculation example:

Hot water flow = 5 L/s (5 kg/s), Cp = 4.18 kJ/kg·K, ΔT = 15 K (from 70°C to 55°C).
Q = 5 × 4.18 × 15 = 313.5 kW of recovered heat. If operates 8 hours/day, 250 days/year → 313.5 × 8 × 250 = 627,000 kWh thermal per year. Saved natural gas (at 90% boiler efficiency) = 627,000 / 0.9 / 10.55 (kWh per m³ of natural gas) ≈ 66,000 m³/year.
4.2.5 Operation Procedure – CHP Unit
Pre-start checks:

Fuel supply valve open, pressure between 0.5–1.0 bar (natural gas) or biomass hopper full.
Cooling water circuit full, no air locks.
Thermal demand exists (e.g., factory needs hot water for laminator pre-heat or space heating). Do not run CHP if thermal demand <30% of output – efficiency drops.
Startup sequence (generic – adapt to manufacturer manual):

Turn on CHP control panel – perform self-test.
Pre-lubricate engine (if applicable).
Initiate start – engine cranks, runs at idle speed.
Allow warm-up (5–10 minutes) until jacket water reaches 70°C.
Synchronise generator to grid (if grid-parallel) or close isolation breaker (island mode).
Gradually increase load to desired power output (e.g., 300 kW). Monitor exhaust temperature – do not exceed limit.
Open heat recovery valve to send hot water to thermal load.
Routine monitoring (every hour):

Electrical output (kW), thermal output (kW), fuel flow rate (Nm³/h or kg/h).
Total efficiency = (kW_elec + kW_thermal) / (fuel_kW_input). Keep >80%.
Engine temperatures (jacket water, exhaust, oil).
Vibration, noise, emissions (visible smoke).
Shutdown (normal):

Reduce electrical load gradually over 2 minutes.
Disconnect from grid (if paralleled).
Run engine at idle for 3 minutes to cool down.
Stop engine. Leave cooling water pump running for 10 minutes to prevent local overheating.
Close fuel valve and log shutdown.
Emergency shutdown: Press emergency stop button. The unit will immediately stop. After restart, contact maintenance to reset alarms.

steps.heading: 4.3 Reduction of Fluorinated Greenhouse Gas (F-Gas) Emissions

body.text: 4.3.1 Understanding F-Gases & Their Impact

Fluorinated gases (HFCs, PFCs, SF₆) are synthetic greenhouse gases used as refrigerants, blowing agents, and electrical insulators. Their Global Warming Potential (GWP) can be thousands of times higher than CO₂ over 100 years:

A 1 kg leak of R410A is equivalent to releasing 2,088 kg of CO₂ – same as driving a car for 5,000 km. Gautam Solar commits to zero uncontrolled emissions through leak prevention and responsible decommissioning.
4.3.2 Inventory & Labelling – Detailed Procedure
Step 1 – Create F-Gas Inventory (Form GS-EN-F04)
For each piece of equipment containing ≥1 kg of F-gas (or any SF₆ amount), record:

Unique ID (e.g., AC-HR-01 for Haridwar, AC-BW-05 for Bhiwani)
Equipment type (split AC, chiller, SF₆ switchgear)
Location (building, room, floor)
Refrigerant/gas type and full chemical name
Factory charge (kg) – from nameplate
Current charge (kg) – after any service
Installation date
Last leak test date and result
Next leak test due date
Step 2 – Labelling

Attach a durable label (weather-proof) near the service valve or on the unit casing stating:

F-GAS (HFC) – DO NOT VENT
Gas: R410A / GWP 2088
Charge: 2.5 kg
CO₂ equivalent: 5,220 kg
Last leak check: [date]

For switchgear with SF₆, label: "SF₆ – Greenhouse gas – report leaks immediately".
4.3.3 Leak Detection & Repair (LDAR) Program
Leak test methods:
Leak test frequency:

rows: Not required by regulation, but check annually (visual)
Annually (using gas detection camera or bagging method)

body.text: Leak threshold & repair timeline:

If measured leak rate >5% of charge per year, repair must be completed within 30 days.
After repair, perform a follow-up leak test to confirm ≤1% leak rate.
Document all repairs, including amount of refrigerant added (if any), in Form GS-EN-F05.
4.3.4 Operational Design to Reduce F-Gas Use
For new purchases (ACs, chillers, refrigerators):

For existing chillers (large systems):
Evaluate retrofit feasibility – some chillers can be converted from R134a to R513A with minor changes (oil compatibility, seals). Require a qualified chiller engineer assessment.
Alternative cooling technologies:

For server rooms, use air-side economizers (free cooling) instead of refrigerant-based AC for many hours in winter.
For small equipment rooms, consider thermosiphon or evaporative cooling (desert coolers) where humidity permits.
4.3.5 Decommissioning & Disposal
When any F-gas equipment is permanently taken out of service (end of life, replacement, or demolition), follow these steps exactly:

Notify Energy Manager and HSE Officer – include equipment ID and refrigerant type.
Recover refrigerant using a certified recovery machine (e.g., Robinair, Appion) and dedicated recovery cylinder (colour-coded: pink for R410A, light blue for R134a, etc.). The technician must hold EPA Section 608 (or equivalent) certification.
Weigh recovered quantity – record in log. If recovered amount is less than nameplate charge by >10%, assume a leak existed; document in NCR.
Send recovered refrigerant to a licensed reclamation or destruction facility – never release to atmosphere, even if "used" or mixed. Obtain a destruction certificate or receipt.
Scrap the equipment only after the compressor/oil has been drained (some oil contains dissolved refrigerant – recover again).
Remove the equipment from the F-Gas Inventory and archive the record with destruction certificate.
Penalty for non-compliance: Any employee found deliberately venting refrigerant will face disciplinary action, and Gautam Solar may be liable for heavy fines under environmental laws.
4.3.6 Training & Awareness

Every maintenance technician who works on AC/refrigeration must complete a certified F-gas handling course within 6 months of hiring.
Annual refresher training (1 hour) covering: identification of leaks, proper use of recovery machine, record keeping.
All employees: awareness poster near AC units: "Report leaks – Save our climate".
4.4 Reduction of IT Infrastructure Energy Consumption
4.4.1 Why IT Energy Matters

Data centres and server rooms consume 10–30 times more energy per square metre than a typical office. A single rack can use 5–10 kW of power, and every 1 kW of IT load requires another 0.5–1 kW for cooling (depending on PUE). Gautam Solar's IT footprint includes:

A small server room at Delhi office (approx. 5 racks)
Network closets at each factory (1–2 racks each)
Approximately 100 desktops/laptops across all sites
UPS, networking, storage
Aggregate IT energy is estimated 8–12% of total office + factory admin load. Reducing it directly lowers electricity bills and carbon footprint.
4.4.2 Server & Data Centre Optimisation – Detailed
A. Virtualisation

Virtualisation runs multiple virtual servers (VMs) on one physical host, reducing the number of physical servers. Each physical server removed saves 150–300 watts continuously (1,300–2,600 kWh/year).

Target: ≥80% of all servers virtualised. Use VMware vSphere, Microsoft Hyper-V, or Proxmox.
Action steps:

Inventory all physical servers – note CPU, RAM, storage utilisation.
Consolidate low-utilisation servers (e.g., <10% CPU) into VMs on a single host.
For remaining physical servers, justify why they cannot be virtualised (e.g., proprietary hardware dongles, real-time requirements). Approval from IT Manager and Energy Manager required.
B. Server power management

Most modern servers support processor C-states (idle power saving). Enable in BIOS:

C1 (halt), C6 (deep sleep). Also enable OS power policies – "Balanced" or "Power Saver" instead of "High Performance" for non-critical servers.

Power capping: For servers with redundant power supplies, set a power cap 10% below nameplate – prevents excess draw.
C. Decommissioning "zombie" servers
A zombie server is one that is powered on but not performing any useful work (e.g., old backup server still plugged in, test server forgotten).

Monthly, run a network scan to list all active IP addresses.
Cross-reference with authorised server list.
For any unauthorised or unknown server, shut it down for 30 days. If no user complains, decommission permanently.
D. Storage optimisation

Replace spinning HDDs (10–15 watts per drive) with SSDs (2–5 watts per drive) for active data. For archiving, use low-power nearline HDDs (5–7 watts) that spin down when idle.
Implement tiered storage: hot data on SSDs, warm data on HDDs, cold data on cloud or tape (if used). Move infrequently accessed files (e.g., >90 days old) to cold tier automatically.
4.4.3 Cooling Optimisation – Detailed (Single largest IT energy saver)
Recommended setpoints (ASHRAE TC 9.9):
Current practice often: 20°C. Raise to 25°C as standard, 27°C if all IT equipment is rated for A3/A4 (most modern gear is). Every 1°C increase saves 3–5% cooling energy.

Hot aisle / cold aisle containment:

Arrange server racks in alternating rows: cold aisle facing the front (intake) and hot aisle facing rear (exhaust). Contain the aisles using blanking panels and door covers to prevent mixing.

Free cooling (air-side economizer):

When outside air temperature is ≤20°C and humidity ≤80% RH, turn off the air conditioner and open motorised dampers to draw outside air through filters into the server room. Exhaust hot air outside. This can be used 2,000–4,000 hours/year in North India (Oct–Feb).
Implementation:

Install a changeover controller with temperature/humidity sensors.
Set changeover: if outside temp < 20°C and inside temp > 24°C → open dampers 50%; if outside < 15°C → 100% free cooling.
4.4.4 UPS Efficiency Improvements

Uninterruptible Power Supplies (UPS) typically operate in double-conversion mode (AC→DC→AC) which wastes 6–10% as heat. When power is stable (most of the time), eco-mode bypasses the inverter, improving efficiency to 97–99%.

Check UPS manufacturer capabilities – many (e.g., Eaton, APC Smart-UPS with "Green Mode") support eco-mode.
Enable eco-mode during working hours when grid quality is good (voltage ±10%, frequency 50 Hz ±1%). Disable during thunderstorms or after grid disturbances.
If the UPS does not support eco-mode, consider replacement when end-of-life. New UPS should have efficiency >94% at 30–80% load.

Right-sizing: A UPS is most efficient at 40–70% load. If a UPS is loaded <20% (common for small server closets), replace with a smaller unit or consolidate loads. Otherwise, the rectifier and inverter losses dominate.
4.4.5 End-User Computing Power Management
Desktop / Laptop policy:

Use Group Policy Object (GPO) for Windows domain or MDM for others:
Turn off monitor after 5 minutes idle.
Put computer to sleep after 15 minutes idle.
Hibernate after 60 minutes (saves state, zero power).
For laptops, also enable "Dim display on battery" and "Lower brightness to 40%".
Educate employees: Shut down or hibernate at end of day. A single PC left on overnight (8 hours) wastes about 0.2 kWh per night → 50 kWh/year per PC. For 100 PCs → 5,000 kWh/year wasted.
Monitor replacement:
Replace any CCFL backlit monitor (older than 2015) with LED backlit – saves 20–30 watts per monitor. New monitors: Energy Star certified with auto-brightness.
Printers & peripherals:

Set printers to deep sleep after 15 minutes – wake only when print job arrives.
Avoid personal printers; use shared MFDs (multi-function devices) which are more efficient per page.
Turn off scanners, external drives when not in use (use USB hubs with individual switches).
4.4.6 Performance Metrics – IT

rows: Total facility energy / IT equipment energy
≤1.5 for server room; ≤1.8 for small closet
Number of VMs / Number of physical hosts
Hours of free cooling / total cooling hours

body.text: How to measure PUE for Gautam Solar server room:

Total energy = UPS input power (from UPS display or sub-meter) + dedicated AC energy (sub-meter).
IT equipment energy = sum of all server, storage, switch nameplate x utilisation (or use UPS output power reading).
Example: UPS output 5 kW, AC draws 1.5 kW → PUE = (5+1.5)/5 = 1.3. Good.

sops.title: Environmental Management, Hazardous Substance Reduction & Emergency Preparedness

blocks.text: This SOP establishes a unified framework at Gautam Solar to:

Reduce material consumption in operations through lightweighting, reuse of reconditioned parts, optimised cutting, and multi-function part design.
Replace hazardous process materials with eco-friendly, bio-based, or low-toxicity alternatives (e.g., plant-based lubricants, non-VOC cleaners, biodegradable logistics materials).
Prepare for environmental emergencies (spills, leaks, equipment failures) involving heavy metals, chlorinated/brominated substances, and other hazardous materials – including communication, testing, and response effectiveness assessment.
Label, store, handle, and transport hazardous substances safely, following GHS standards, using spill-proof containers, safety signs, and exposure reduction equipment.
Treat and dispose of hazardous waste safely, ensuring neutralisation or irreversible transformation, with regular inspections and regulatory compliance.
Reduce or eliminate hazardous substances in operations by substituting heavy metals, halogenated compounds, and toxic solvents with greener alternatives (lead-free, recyclable, biodegradable, eco-friendly flame retardants).
Comply with the Stockholm Convention on POPs by substituting or modifying processes to minimise release, and destroying any POPs-containing waste.
Comply with the Minamata Convention on Mercury by replacing mercury-containing equipment, implementing closed-loop systems, and upgrading capture/treatment technologies.
This SOP applies to process materials (consumables used in production and operations) and hazardous waste generated, but excludes finished product materials and primary packaging (covered elsewhere).
The SOP covers all Gautam Solar sites and all relevant activities:

rows: Production (cell cutting, ribbon slitting, frame cutting, soldering), maintenance (reconditioned parts), design (multi-function parts, lightweighting), warehousing (nesting, pack optimisation).
Lubricants for soldering machines, degreasers for cleaning glass/cells, cleaners for maintenance, internal logistics (biodegradable stretch wrap, reusable pallets).
Spill response for coolants, soldering fluxes, cleaning solvents, battery acids, chlorinated cleaning agents, brominated flame retardants (if stored), heavy metal residues from cells.
Hazardous substance labelling, storage, handling, transport
All chemicals with GHS hazard pictograms: fluxes, solvents, adhesives, sealants, cleaning agents, compressed gases, acids, bases, etc.
Spent solvents, used oil, contaminated rags, chemical containers, cell breakage residues (trace heavy metals), expired chemicals.
Lead-free solders, halogen-free flame retardants (in j-boxes, cables), non-toxic fluxes, water-based cleaners, biodegradable lubricants.
Identify any POPs (e.g., certain flame retardants, pesticides – unlikely but check cleaning agents). Modify processes to avoid release; destroy POPs waste.
Replace mercury-containing thermometers, pressure gauges, fluorescent lamps (with LED), switches, relays. Install mercury capture in waste gas if any.

blocks.text: Exclusions: Finished solar modules (product materials), primary packaging for shipment, office supplies.

responsibilities: Overall owner of this SOP; maintains chemical inventory; leads emergency response team; conducts inspections and audits.
Implements material reduction initiatives (cutting optimisation, part reuse). Approves substitution of process materials.
Purchases only eco-friendly / bio-based alternatives from approved list; obtains SDS and GHS labels.
Ensures proper labelling, storage (secondary containment), transport (spill-proof packaging). Maintains hazardous substance register.
Handles reconditioned parts; replaces mercury-containing equipment; supervises waste treatment.
Trained members (at each site) who execute spill control, first aid, and evacuation during environmental emergencies.
Report leaks/spills immediately; use hazardous substances only as trained; follow labelling and storage rules.

steps.heading: 4.1 Reduction of Material Consumption in Operations

body.text: 4.1.1 Lightweighting & Multi-function Parts. Objective: Reduce the quantity of metals, plastics, and other materials used in manufacturing without compromising product quality.

rows: Redesign aluminium frame cross-section while maintaining mechanical strength.
Switch from 35mm to 30mm frame thickness for certain module sizes, saving 15% aluminium per unit.
Use narrower interconnector ribbons without increasing resistance.
Reduce ribbon width from 1.5 mm to 1.2 mm – saves 20% copper per module.
Combine two or more functions into a single moulded part.
Integrate junction box base and cable strain relief into one moulding, eliminating separate plastic bracket.
Use 3.2 mm instead of 4.0 mm where permitted by mechanical load standards.
For rooftop modules not subject to heavy snow, 3.2 mm tempered glass saves 20% glass weight.

body.text:
R&D / Engineering team evaluates each component annually for lightweighting potential.
Prototype and test (mechanical load, thermal cycling, humidity freeze per IEC 61215).
Once validated, update BOM and procurement specifications.
Objective: Maximise yield from raw materials (cells, glass, EVA, backsheet, ribbon). For solar cells (slicing / dicing):

Use laser cutting instead of mechanical scribing to reduce kerf loss (less material wasted as dust).
Optimise cell layout for half-cut or third-cut cells – minimise edge waste.
For EVA/backsheet rolls:

Calculate optimal cut length to match module dimensions with minimal roll remnant.
Use software (nesting algorithm) to combine different module sizes from same roll.
For ribbon / busbar:

Use reel-to-reel feeding with sensor to stop precisely at required length, avoiding over-cut waste.
Recycle trimmed ends (copper scrap – sent to authorised recycler).

Production planner reviews cut yield monthly.
Any process generating >3% scrap material triggers a Kaizen event to reduce waste.

steps.heading: 4.1.3 Integration of Reused or Reconditioned Parts

body.text: Objective: Reduce consumption of new parts by refurbishing and reusing components from returned modules (rework) or from internal process waste. Allowed reconditioned parts (after rigorous testing):

rows: Clean terminals, replace gasket, test IP rating
Straighten in press, re-anodise if needed

body.text: Prohibited: Never reuse cells (even if electrically good) – risk of hidden microcracks. Use only new cells. Procedure for reconditioning:

Collect eligible parts from reject modules or production waste.
Send to designated rework station with trained technician.
Perform reconditioning as per work instruction.
Test using the same criteria as new parts.
Label “RECONDITIONED – QUALIFIED” with date and technician ID.
Reconditioned parts are used only for internal repairs or low-priority orders (customer approval if required).
Tracking: Maintain a log of reconditioned parts used, showing material saved (kg) per month.
Calculate Material Intensity (kg per kWp of module) monthly. Target reduction of 3% year-on-year.

steps.heading: 4.2 Use of Eco-friendly or Bio-based Process Materials

body.text: 4.2.1 Replacement of Petroleum-based Lubricants. Current use: Mineral oil-based lubricants for soldering machine moving parts, conveyor chains, and pneumatic cylinders. Alternatives:

Plant-based hydraulic oils (e.g., rapeseed oil ester) – biodegradable, non-toxic.
Synthetic esters derived from renewable feedstocks.

Procurement to source bio-based lubricant that meets equipment manufacturer specifications (viscosity, oxidation stability).
Test on one machine for 500 hours, check wear debris and temperature.
If successful, roll out to all machines. Document in GS-EN-F09 (Eco-material substitution log).
4.2.2 Substitution of VOCs / Solvents. Current use: Isopropyl alcohol (IPA), acetone, or toluene for cleaning glass edges, cells, and machine parts. Alternatives:

Water-based degreasers (low VOC, typically <5%).
Citrus-based terpene cleaners (derived from orange peels) – effective for flux residues.
Pressurised CO₂ cleaning (dry ice blasting) – no chemical waste.

Evaluate cleaning effectiveness using contact angle measurement or residue test.
Switch to water-based cleaner for routine cleaning; keep small quantity of IPA only for critical applications (approved by HSE).
Train operators on proper dilution and disposal (water-based cleaner can go to drain only if pH neutral and no heavy metals – confirm with local ETP).
4.2.3 Biodegradable / Renewable Materials for Internal Logistics. Objective: Replace single-use plastics and non-renewable materials in warehousing and internal transport.

rows: Biodegradable stretch film (e.g., based on PBAT + PLA)
Reusable wooden pallets from FSC-certified timber, or recycled plastic pallets
Corrugated cardboard padding or molded pulp
Jute or biodegradable strapping (for light loads)

body.text:
Inventory all single-use logistics materials.
For each, identify an alternative that is either reusable, recyclable, or biodegradable.
Conduct cost and performance comparison (e.g., load stability, tear resistance).
Phase in alternatives over 12 months. Track quantity of non-renewable plastic reduced (kg/month).
4.3.1 Identification of Potential Environmental Emergencies. At Gautam Solar sites, the following scenarios could cause environmental harm:

rows: Cell breakage (trace heavy metals – silver, lead, tin)
Cooling water additives (corrosion inhibitors – may contain chlorinated compounds)
Oil contamination of floor wash water

body.text:
Conduct a Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA) for environmental aspects annually.
For each scenario with potential impact severity “High”, develop a specific Emergency Response Plan (ERP).
4.3.2 Emergency Response Plans & Documentation. Each site maintains a Site-Specific ERP with the following sections:

Emergency contact list (internal: HSE Manager, ERT leader; external: fire brigade, pollution control board, nearest hospital).
Spill response procedure (step-by-step for small vs. large spills).
Spill kit locations (marked on site map).
Evacuation routes and assembly points.
Communication protocol (who notifies which authority, when).
Post-incident assessment (root cause analysis, corrective actions).
Revisions: The ERP is reviewed and revised:

Annually (scheduled).
After any actual environmental emergency.
After any change in operations (new chemicals, new equipment).
Revisions are documented in a Revision Log (Appendix A) and communicated to all employees via email and notice board.
4.3.3 Testing of Emergency Procedures & Equipment. Schedule:

Drill documentation: Use GS-EN-F10 – Emergency Drill Report (date, scenario, participants, time to respond, observations, corrective actions). After each drill, conduct a hot wash (immediate feedback session) and update the ERP if gaps are found.
4.3.4 Effectiveness Assessment of Response. After any real emergency (or major drill), the HSE Manager leads a Post-Incident Effectiveness Assessment:

Response time vs. target (e.g., spill contained within 10 minutes).
Proper use of PPE and spill kits (observed).
Communication effectiveness (were external authorities notified correctly?).
Environmental impact (was any contamination measured? soil/water samples if needed).
Corrective actions (update training, repair equipment, revise ERP).
Results recorded in GS-EN-F11 – Emergency Response Effectiveness Report. Share summary with management quarterly.

steps.heading: 4.4 Labeling, Storage, Handling & Transport of Hazardous Substances

body.text: 4.4.1 Labeling (GHS Compliant). Requirement: Every container of hazardous process material (original or secondary) must have a GHS label (Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals). Label elements (minimum):

rows: H225 (Highly flammable), H319 (Causes serious eye irritation)
P210 (Keep away from heat), P280 (Wear gloves/eye protection)

body.text:
All incoming chemicals must have original GHS label. Reject unlabelled drums.
For secondary containers (e.g., spray bottles, small dispensers), attach a durable GHS label with same information.
Store responsible (HSE) conducts weekly labelling inspection using GS-EN-F12 (Hazardous Substance Label Check).
4.4.2 Storage – Spill Prevention & Segregation. Requirements:

Secondary containment: All liquid hazardous substances >5 litres must be stored on spill pallets (integral sump) or in bunded areas. Capacity of secondary containment must be ≥110% of largest container.
Segregation: Incompatible chemicals stored separately (e.g., acids away from bases, oxidisers away from flammables). Use chemical compatibility chart (Appendix B).
Ventilation: Flammable storage cabinet must be vented to outside.
Temperature control: Store solvents away from heat sources; refrigerated storage for peroxidisable chemicals.
Limit quantities: No more than 200 litres of flammable liquid outside of flammable cabinet.
Procedure for storage area inspection (monthly):

Check for leaks, rust, damaged containers.
Verify spill pallet drain valve is closed.
Ensure fire extinguisher (foam or CO₂) is present and inspected.
Record on GS-EN-F13 – Hazardous Storage Inspection Log.
4.4.3 Handling – Exposure Reduction. Engineering controls:

rows: Local exhaust ventilation (LEV) at dispensing point
Drip trays under drums; self-closing taps
Drum trolley, pallet lifter, overhead crane
Protective barriers (splash guards) around dispensing area

body.text:
Safe work procedure (SWP) for each hazardous substance (available near point of use).
Mandatory PPE as per SDS (e.g., nitrile gloves, chemical goggles, apron, face shield).
No eating/drinking in storage or handling areas.
Procedure for handling:

Operator reviews SWP before starting task.
Checks that LEV is operating (airflow indicator).
Puts on required PPE (inspection checklist: GS-EN-F14).
Uses sealed dispensing system (pump or tap) – no open pouring.
Immediately cleans any spill with spill kit.
Records any incidents in near-miss log.
4.4.4 Transport – On-site & Off-site. On-site transport (between stores and production):

Use sealed, spill-proof secondary containers (e.g., chemical-resistant tote or cart with drip tray).
For drums, use drum dolly with strap – never roll on floor.
Establish designated route that avoids pedestrian heavy areas.
Off-site transport (supply to Gautam Solar, or disposal to vendor):

Only authorised transporters with valid hazardous material (HAZMAT) license.
Packaging must comply with UN certification (e.g., UN 1H1 for plastic drums).
Shipping documents include proper shipping name, UN number, class, packing group, and emergency contact.
Procedure for receiving:

Before unloading, verify packaging integrity (no leaks).
Check that SDS accompanies shipment.
Reject any leaking or damaged containers.
4.4.5 Safety Signs & Employee Instructions. Post the following signs at all hazardous substance storage and handling areas:

“GHS Hazard Pictograms” (reference chart)
“Chemical Spill Procedure” (simplified flow chart)
“Wear PPE” (with pictograms of required gear)
“Emergency Contact” numbers
“No Smoking / No Open Flames”

Employee training: Initial training on hazardous substance management (2 hours) for all operators handling chemicals. Refresher annually including a short written assessment. Training records maintained by HSE (GS-EN-F15).

steps.heading: 4.5 Treatment & Safe Disposal of Hazardous Waste

body.text: 4.5.1 Identification of Hazardous Waste Streams

columns: Classification (as per Hazardous Waste Management Rules, India)

body.text: 4.5.2 Treatment Procedures. On-site treatment (where permitted and safe)

rows: Recovered solvent used as cleaning fluid; residue as fuel blend

body.text: Note: Only trained personnel with proper equipment (still, neutralisation tank) may perform on-site treatment. All treatment steps must be logged (GS-EN-F16 – Hazardous Waste Treatment Log). For wastes not treated on-site: Send to authorised Common Hazardous Waste Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facility (CHWTSDF) or authorised recycler.
5.3 Safe Disposal Protocols. Procedure for off-site disposal:

Accumulate hazardous waste in labelled, sealed containers in a dedicated hazardous waste storage area (bunded, under roof, with spill kit).
Quantity limit: Do not store more than 1,000 kg or 3 months’ generation (whichever lower).
Manifest: Prepare Form 9 (as per Hazardous Waste Rules) for each shipment.
Authorised transporter: Use only registered vehicles with GPS tracking.
Disposal facility: Verify CHWTSDF license and that they use approved methods (incineration with flue gas cleaning, stabilisation/solidification, secured landfill).
Obtain disposal certificate – proof that waste was received and treated (retain for 5 years).
Prohibited actions:

No dilution of hazardous waste with non-hazardous waste.
No dumping in municipal landfill.
No burning in open.
No discharge to drain unless treated to permissible limits (consent from State Pollution Control Board).
4.5.4 Inspections of Hazardous Waste Management
Findings recorded in GS-EN-F17 – Hazardous Waste Inspection Report. Non-conformances must be corrected within 7 days.

steps.heading: 4.6 Reduction of Hazardous Substances through Greener Alternatives

body.text: 4.6.1 Replacement of Heavy Metals & Halogenated Compounds. Current hazardous substances (examples):

rows: Cell tabbing and stringing (lead-based solder alloy)
Some older cable materials (now phased out)

body.text: Greener alternatives:

rows: Lead-free solder (Sn96.5/Ag3.0/Cu0.5 – SAC305) or Sn100C (with nickel/germanium)
No lead; slightly higher melting point but acceptable for PV
Phosphorus-based (e.g., resorcinol bis(diphenyl phosphate) – RDP) or aluminium trihydroxide (non-halogenated)
Water-soluble organic acids (citric, succinic) instead of halogenated activators
Water-based or terpene-based instead of chlorinated solvents (e.g., trichloroethylene)
No chlorinated VOCs, no ozone depletion

body.text: Procedure for substitution:

Engineering and HSE identify a candidate replacement.
Review SDS and compare hazard profile (GHS statements).
Test performance (solder joint strength, flame retardancy rating UL94 V-0).
Obtain management approval (Production, QA, HSE).
Update purchasing specifications to exclude the hazardous substance.
Train operators on new material.
Tracking: Maintain GS-EN-F18 – Hazardous Substance Substitution Log, listing replaced substance, new substance, date, and quantity of hazardous material eliminated (kg/year).
4.6.2 Lead-Free Initiative. Target: All new soldering processes to be lead-free by [target date – e.g., 31 December 2026]. Transition plan:

Phase 1: Evaluate lead-free solder on one stringer machine (adjust temperature profile, test peel strength, EL images).
Phase 2: Train operators on handling (higher temperature requires different flux and longer dwell time).
Phase 3: Roll out to all production lines.
Phase 4: Dispose of lead-containing solder waste via authorised recycler.
4.6.3 Eco-friendly Flame Retardants. For any new purchase of junction boxes, connectors, or cable trays:

Specify halogen-free flame retardant (HF-FR) meeting IEC 61249-2-21 (halogen content <1500 ppm Cl, Br, total <1500 ppm).
Prefer phosphinate or phosphonate based FRs.

4.7 POPs (Stockholm Convention) Compliance. 4.7.1 Identification of POPs in Process Materials. Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) relevant to solar manufacturing (historical uses – most are already restricted):

rows: Check SDS for any fluorinated surfactant – substitute.

body.text:
HSE Manager maintains a POPs Declaration from all chemical suppliers (form GS-EN-F19), confirming that their product does not contain any POPs listed in the Stockholm Convention (current annexes A, B, C).
For any material that may contain POPs (e.g., legacy stock), send a sample to accredited lab for analysis.
If POPs found > 50 ppm (threshold), quarantine the material and cease use.

4.7.2 Process Modification to Limit POPs Release. Even if no POPs are intentionally used, some processes could generate POPs as by-products (e.g., incomplete combustion of chlorinated materials). At Gautam Solar, no combustion processes exist, so risk is very low. However: Ensure that any thermal treatment of waste (if done on-site) operates at >1000°C with sufficient residence time to destroy any POPs – but Gautam Solar does not incinerate waste. All hazardous waste sent to CHWTSDF where incinerators are designed for POPs destruction.

4.7.3 Management of Waste Containing POPs. If waste is classified as hazardous due to POPs (e.g., old cables with decaBDE), it must be destroyed or irreversibly transformed so that it no longer persists. Allowed methods per Stockholm Convention:

High-temperature incineration (>1100°C with residence time >2 seconds).
Plasma arc treatment.
Cement kiln co-processing with proper gas cleaning.

Label the waste “CONTAINS POPS – DESTRUCTION REQUIRED”.
Send only to a facility with authorisation for POPs waste destruction.
Obtain certificate of destruction (including destruction efficiency >99.9999%).
Record in GS-EN-F20 – POPs Waste Management Log.
4.8 Mercury (Minamata Convention) Compliance. 4.8.1 Mercury-Containing Equipment Inventory. Gautam Solar identifies and replaces mercury-containing devices:

Conduct site-wide audit using GS-EN-F21 – Mercury Equipment Inventory.
For each item, record type, quantity, mercury content (from manufacturer or estimate), and location.
For lights: Replace all fluorescent and CFL with LED as they burn out or within 2 years (whichever earlier).
For thermometers / gauges: Immediate replacement (cost low, risk high if breakage).
Securely store removed mercury-containing devices in unbreakable, sealed container labelled “Hazardous Waste – Mercury”.
4.8.2 Mercury Capture & Treatment. No intentional use of mercury in solar manufacturing. However, if a mercury device breaks (e.g., fluorescent tube shatters), follow this mercury spill procedure:

Evacuate area immediately.
Open windows for ventilation.
Do not use vacuum cleaner (spreads mercury vapour).
Use mercury spill kit (sulphur powder or special absorbent) to collect visible droplets.
Place all contaminated materials (rags, powder, broken glass) into a sealed plastic bag labelled “MERCURY WASTE”.
Send waste to authorised mercury recycler / CHWTSDF that can recover mercury.

Closed-loop systems: Not applicable to mercury at Gautam Solar (no mercury-using processes). But for completeness, if any mercury-containing equipment is used (e.g., old rectifiers), they must be enclosed with local exhaust ventilation to capture any vapour. 4.8.3 Process Optimisation to Eliminate Mercury. Wherever mercury was used in analytical equipment (e.g., mercury porosimeter – not present), switch to alternative techniques (gas adsorption, pycnometry). Ensure that any third-party laboratory used for testing does not use mercury-based analytical methods for Gautam Solar samples. Compliance statement: Gautam Solar certifies that it does not use mercury in any manufacturing process and has replaced all mercury-containing equipment at its facilities (or is on a documented phase-out schedule). This is aligned with the Minamata Convention on Mercury (ratified by India in 2018).
