sops.title: Integrated Waste Management and Resource Recovery

blocks.text: This SOP establishes a comprehensive framework at Gautam Solar to:

Reduce internal waste generation through reuse, recovery of scrap metal, equipment, electronic components, and repurposing of used infrastructure.
Sort operational waste into distinct streams (organic, paper, glass, metals, plastics, hazardous waste, e-waste) using labeled bins and partnerships with waste management companies.
Implement waste stream mapping – a systematic analysis tracking each waste type from generation to final disposal, identifying efficiency gaps and improvement opportunities.
Refurbish IT equipment (computers, monitors, servers, phones) to extend useful life, reduce electronic waste, using internal or third-party specialists.
Sort internal electronic waste (used IT equipment, batteries, phones, cables) separately from other waste, with clear guidelines and partnerships with authorised e-waste recyclers.

This SOP covers waste generated from Gautam Solar’s own operations (offices, factories, warehouses) and explicitly excludes waste from products manufactured by the company (end-of-life solar panels – covered under a separate product stewardship SOP).
The SOP applies to all waste generated at all three Gautam Solar sites:

rows: Aluminium frame offcuts, copper ribbon trims, steel from old racks, tin/lead solder dross
Old circuit boards from decommissioned equipment, sensors, relays, power supplies
Old laminator parts, conveyor rollers, pneumatic cylinders, pumps
Food waste (canteen), paper/cardboard, glass bottles, plastic packaging, general non-hazardous
Used oil, spent solvents, chemical containers, contaminated rags
End-of-life computers, laptops, monitors, printers, UPS batteries, mobile phones, network switches

blocks.text:
Waste generated from manufacturing processes that is already covered under hazardous waste disposal (GS-EN-002 Section 4.5) – but this SOP will include cross-references for consistency.
Finished solar modules at end of life (not applicable to internal operations).

responsibilities: Overall owner of this SOP; conducts waste stream mapping annually; reports waste reduction metrics to management.
Manages office waste segregation (paper, plastic, organic); contracts waste collection vendors.
Implements scrap metal recovery and repurposing of used equipment; tracks weight of recyclable metals.
Oversees IT equipment refurbishment program; maintains inventory of retired IT assets; coordinates with third-party refurbishers/e-waste recyclers.
Provides labeled bins and containers; ensures waste is stored in designated areas before collection.
Follow waste segregation instructions; place waste in correct bins; report any improper disposal.

body.text: Objective: Recover valuable metals (aluminium, copper, steel, tin) from production and maintenance activities, sending them to authorised recyclers instead of landfill.

rows: Hazardous? Lead-containing → hazardous waste; lead-free → recyclable (check local rules)

body.text: Procedure for scrap metal management:

rows: Place dedicated metal scrap bins (colour-coded: blue for aluminium, yellow for copper, grey for steel) at each production area.
Operators discard offcuts and trimmings into the correct bin immediately after cutting. Do not mix with general waste.
At end of each shift, weigh each bin using platform scale. Record weight in GS-WM-F01 – Scrap Metal Log.
When bin is full, transfer to secured scrap storage area (locked cage to prevent theft).
Weekly, authorised scrap dealer collects. Issue receipt with weight and payment.
Reconcile monthly: total scrap sold vs. expected yield (calculated from raw material input). Investigate discrepancies >5%.

body.text: Target: Recover 90% of all ferrous and non-ferrous metal waste. Track metal recycling rate = (kg recycled) / (kg generated) × 100%.
Objective: Extend life of components removed from decommissioned machines, repairing and reusing them in other equipment or as spare parts.

rows: Test windings, replace bearings → reuse on conveyor or fan
Clean contacts, test coil → use as spare for older machines
Replace capacitors → reuse for control panels
Clean lens, test output → reuse on other lines
Replace seals → reuse for non-critical actuation
Re-grease, replace bearing → reuse on new conveyor section

body.text: Procedure – Reuse program:

rows: When equipment is decommissioned, Maintenance performs teardown and inspection using GS-WM-F02 – Component Reuse Assessment.
Assess each component: visual, functional test (e.g., motor winding resistance, contactor coil continuity).

Classify as: Reusable as is – clean, test, label, store in designated “Reusable Spares” cabinet. Repairable – send to workshop for refurbishment (replace bearings, seals, capacitors). Not reusable – send to scrap metal or e-waste stream.
Tag each reusable component with “RECONDITIONED – TESTED” and date.
Update spare parts inventory system to include reconditioned parts at zero cost (but tracked for performance).
When a machine needs a replacement, first check reconditioned stock before purchasing new.

body.text: Performance metric: Number of reconditioned components reused per month, and cost saved (new purchase cost avoided). Report quarterly.
Objective: Give old equipment a second life in a different role rather than scrapping.

rows: Old stringer machine (no longer meets speed/quality standards)
Use as training simulator for new operators (no production, only practice).
Remove heating elements, use as manual layup table or vacuum press for small R&D samples.
Use as storage shelving in warehouse.
Repair and reuse for internal material transport; if beyond repair, chip for biomass fuel (if permitted) or send to authorised recycler.

body.text:
When a major asset is retired, the Department Head (Production/IT/Admin) completes a Repurposing Evaluation Form (GS-WM-F03).
Evaluate if the asset can be safely and usefully redeployed elsewhere in Gautam Solar (or donated to a technical school/NGO).
If repurposing is approved, update asset register and physically relocate with proper cleaning/safety checks.
If not repurposable, then proceed to disassembly for component reuse (Section 4.1.2) and then recycling.

Donation: For equipment that is functional but no longer needed (e.g., old computers after refurbishment, office furniture), donate to local schools or charities. Document donation with acknowledgment letter (GS-WM-F04). This avoids waste and benefits community.

sections.title: Operational Waste Sorting into Respective Streams

body.text: Gautam Solar implements source segregation at all sites. Employees separate waste into the following streams:

rows: Canteen leftovers, fruit peels, coffee grounds
Sent to compost facility or organic waste converter (if on-site)
Office paper, newspaper, cardboard boxes, corrugated sheets
Crushed and sent to glass recycler
Aluminium cans, metal caps, small scrap
PET bottles, HDPE containers (clean), plastic packaging film
Dirty paper, multi-layer packaging, food-soiled items, sanitary waste
Used oil, spent solvents, chemical containers, contaminated rags, batteries
Stored separately, sent to CHWTSDF (per GS-EN-002)
Old cables, chargers, small electronic components, toner cartridges, UPS batteries

body.text: Requirements:

Each bin must have a clear, durable label showing:
Waste stream name and colour code.
Pictograms (universal symbols for paper, plastic, glass, etc.).
List of acceptable items and common contaminants (e.g., “No food-soiled paper in paper bin”).
Bins are placed at convenient locations:
Each workstation (production) – small metal/plastic bins.
Break rooms and canteen – organic, paper, plastic, general.
Office corridors – paper, plastic, general.
Near printer/copier – paper bin (for misprints).
Chemical storage area – hazardous waste bin.
Inspection:

Daily: Housekeeping team checks that bins are used correctly.
Weekly: HSE or Admin reviews contamination (e.g., food waste in paper bin). Contaminated bins trigger retraining for that department.
Selection criteria for vendors:

rows: Consent from State Pollution Control Board (SPCB)

body.text:
HSE maintains an Approved Waste Vendor List (GS-WM-F05) with contact details, license numbers, and validity dates.
Contracts include performance clauses: vendor must provide weight receipt and disposal certificate for each collection.
Quarterly, HSE conducts a vendor audit (desk review of their compliance, no need to visit unless high risk).

Waste stream mapping is a visual and analytical tool that tracks a specific waste type from its point of generation (e.g., production line, office desk) to its final destination (recycling, incineration, landfill). It helps identify inefficiencies: unnecessary handling steps, mixing of incompatible wastes, missing bins, or costly disposal routes.
For each major waste stream, Gautam Solar will create a “Waste Stream Map” (see example below).

rows: Select a waste stream (e.g., aluminium scrap from frame cutting).
Walk the physical flow: observe where waste is generated, collected, stored, transported, and finally disposed.
Interview operators and storekeepers: “What happens to this waste? Are there delays? Is it ever mixed with other waste?”
Measure quantities at each stage (weigh at generation, weigh after storage, weigh at dispatch).
Identify gaps: e.g., “Scrap bin not labeled → operators put aluminium into general waste” or “No dedicated metal bin in cutting area → scrap ends up in plastic bin”.
Create final Waste Stream Map using standard symbols (see Appendix A).
Implement improvements and re-map after 6 months to verify progress.

body.text: Stream: Aluminium frame cutting scrap at Haridwar Factory
rows: Frame cutting machine produces scrap ends (5–10 cm pieces).
Operator sweeps scrap into open tub (no label). Sometimes metal and plastic mixed.
Tub placed near machine. Plastic scrap from packaging also thrown in.
Forklift takes tub to scrap cage.
Scrap cage (aluminium only). But plastic contamination requires manual sorting.
Recycler collects, pays by weight of pure aluminium.
Paid only for net Al, contamination reduces revenue

body.text: Identified improvements:

Install labeled blue bin for aluminium scrap directly at cutting machine.
Train operators to discard only aluminium (no plastic packaging).
Install a tray to capture all small pieces (reduce 5% loss).
Expected improvement: +15 kg/week recovered, +₹X revenue, less labour sorting.
Mapping frequency: Each major waste stream mapped annually (or after any process change). Completed maps stored in GS-WM-F06 – Waste Stream Mapping Records.

narrative.text: The HSE Manager uses maps to calculate waste diversion rate:
Diversion rate = (Total waste recycled + reused + composted) / (Total waste generated) × 100%
Target diversion rate: ≥75% by end of Year 2 (excluding hazardous waste which is treated, not landfilled).
Areas with low diversion (e.g., general waste >20%) trigger a Kaizen event to reduce contamination or find new recycling options.

body.text: Refurbishment extends the useful life of computers, laptops, monitors, servers, and peripherals. It is preferred over recycling because it avoids the energy and material cost of manufacturing new devices. Gautam Solar will implement a tiered approach:

rows: Keep in use or re-deploy to another department
Tier 2 – Minor issues (slow performance, dead battery, cracked screen but functional)
Refurbish internally or via third party – replace battery, upgrade RAM/SSD, reinstall OS.
Use for less demanding roles (e.g., training room, warehouse terminal) or donate to schools.
Tier 3 – Major issues (motherboard failure, broken hinges, obsolete)
Part out – salvage RAM, hard drive, screen, keyboard as spares. Remaining carcass to e-waste recycler.
Tier 4 – Beyond repair (physically crushed, water damage)
Direct to e-waste recycler for material recovery (metals, plastics, glass).

body.text: Internal refurbishment (for basic upgrades):

rows: IT department maintains an IT Asset Retirement Log (GS-WM-F07) for all devices removed from service.
Assess device: run diagnostics (memory test, hard drive health, battery cycle count).

If candidate for refurbishment: Clean internally (dust removal) and externally. Replace worn parts: battery, keyboard, fan, thermal paste. Upgrade: add SSD, increase RAM (if cost-effective). Wipe hard drive using secure erase (DBAN or manufacturer tool). Install fresh OS (Windows or Linux lightweight). Perform full test (24 hours burn-in).
Apply a sticker “REFURBISHED BY GAUTAM SOLAR – [Date]”.
Re-deploy internally (to another department) or list for donation.

body.text: Third-party refurbishment partnership:

Gautam Solar may partner with an authorised e-waste refurbisher (e.g., certified by R2 or e-Stewards) for complex repairs or large volumes.
The partner must provide a certificate stating that:
All data has been destroyed.
Refurbished devices meet functional standards.
Any non-refurbishable parts are recycled responsibly.
Maintain records of devices sent for third-party refurbishment (GS-WM-F08).

After internal needs are met, working refurbished equipment can be donated to:
Government schools (computer labs).
Non-profit organisations (NGOs).
Technical training institutes.
Donation procedure:

Obtain written request from recipient.
Prepare device (data wipe, install basic software).
Issue donation letter (GS-WM-F09) with list of items and “no warranty, as-is” disclaimer.
Recipient signs acknowledgment. This counts as waste diversion (not landfilled).
Tax benefits: Eligible under CSR spending (India). Coordinate with finance.

rows: (Months from first use to final recycling)
≥5 years for laptops, ≥7 years for desktops
Number of devices refurbished / Total devices retired
Weight of devices refurbished & donated (kg) avoided from recycling

sections.title: Sorting & Management of Internal Electronic Waste (E-Waste)

body.text: For the purpose of this SOP, internal e-waste means:

All electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) used by Gautam Solar that has reached end-of-life, excluding the solar modules we manufacture.
Examples: Computers, laptops, monitors, printers, scanners, UPS units (including batteries), network switches, routers, mobile phones, landline phones, cables, chargers, power supplies, electronic lab equipment (multimeters, oscilloscopes), worn-out batteries (Li-ion, lead-acid, NiMH), toner cartridges, CD/DVDs.

This excludes hazardous waste batteries that are already covered under hazardous waste stream (lead-acid batteries) – but they should be segregated as e-waste or hazardous waste according to local rules. In India, batteries are covered under Batteries (Management and Handling) Rules; for simplicity, Gautam Solar will send all batteries (except alkaline disposables) to authorised e-waste / battery recycler.
Collection bins/containers:
Placement:

Each office floor: small e-waste bin near printer/copy room.
IT server room: dedicated e-waste area for retired servers, network gear.
Factory maintenance shop: battery bin and small e-waste bin.
Warehouse: large pallet for bulk e-waste (old UPS units, etc.).
Clear instructions (to be posted near e-waste bins):
DO PUT in e-waste bin:

Broken / old cables, chargers, adapters
Dead batteries (tape terminals of Li-ion)
Non-working mice, keyboards, webcams
Old mobile phones, landline phones
UPS batteries (place carefully, avoid acid spill – use secondary tray)
Toner cartridges (keep in original bag to avoid dust)
DO NOT PUT:

General office paper, plastic, food waste
Working equipment (first try refurbishment – contact IT)
Large appliances (e.g., broken AC – call maintenance separately)

blocks.text: 4.1 Water Reclamation & Internal Reuse

body.text:
In solar panel manufacturing, water is primarily used for:

Cleaning glass sheets before lamination,
Cooling circulating systems for laminators and curing ovens,
Washing floors and equipment,
Domestic purposes (canteens, toilets).

Reclaiming water reduces pressure on local water bodies and lowers operational costs. Gautam Solar will target a water reuse rate of ≥50% within two years and explore Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) as a long-term goal.

rows: Ultrafiltration or microfiltration removes suspended solids, colloids, and bacteria. It produces high-quality effluent suitable for reuse in non-critical applications.
Pre-treatment for RO; polishing of secondary effluent before reuse.
RO removes dissolved salts, heavy metals, and organic compounds, producing almost pure water. Brine (concentrate) requires further handling.
Production of demineralised water for precision cleaning; recycling of cooling tower blowdown.
A ZLD system combines RO, evaporation, and crystallisation to recover up to 95–99% of water as distillate. Only solid salts remain for safe disposal.
Long-term target for both factories to eliminate liquid effluent discharge.
Uses ion-exchange membranes to separate charged ions (e.g., salts, heavy metals) from wastewater. It is energy-efficient for low-to-medium salinity streams.
Potential for treating specific heavy-metal-bearing streams (e.g., from soldering flux washes).

body.text: Before designing any reclamation system, the following sources must be characterised:

rows: Fine glass particles, dust, traces of cleaning agents
Rinsing again after proper filtration; floor washing

Collect wastewater from designated streams (e.g., cooling tower blowdown, glass rinse) into a collection sump.
Pass through primary physical treatment (screen, grit chamber) to remove large solids and debris.
Apply chemical coagulation and flocculation to aggregate fine suspended particles.
Clarify in a settling tank; sludge is dewatered and disposed as per hazardous waste rules (if heavy metals present).
Route clarified water to membrane filtration (UF/RO) for polishing. Ensure RO membranes are periodically cleaned.
Direct permeate (treated water) to a reuse storage tank. Monitor water quality (turbidity, conductivity, pH) weekly.
Reuse the reclaimed water for compatible operations: cooling tower make-up, floor washing, gardening, toilet flushing.
Manage the RO concentrate / brine by evaporation (in ZLD) or sending to an authorised Common Effluent Treatment Plant (CETP).

steps.heading: Steps of a Comprehensive Water Audit

rows: Form a cross-functional team (HSE, Production, Maintenance). Define scope (whole factory or specific zones). Gather 12–24 months of water bills, plumbing layouts, as-built drawings. Establish baseline (litres per module).

Verify flow meter placement and calibration. Map end-uses: cooling towers, washing stations, domestic, landscaping, fire systems. Use ultrasonic/acoustic tools to locate hidden leaks. Measure flow rates with bucket & stopwatch where necessary.

Account for all inflows (municipal, borewell, rainwater) and outflows (evaporation, discharge, reuse). Calculate real losses (leaks, overflows) and apparent losses (metering errors, unauthorised use). Create a water balance diagram.
Compare with industry benchmarks (e.g., litres per module) and Indian standards (IS 17408). Identify water-intensive equipment and over-consumed areas.

Design & Components
Rainwater harvesting captures and stores rainwater from rooftops and paved areas for later use. The system consists of:

steps.heading: 4.5 Reduction of Heavy Metal Discharges in Wastewater

body.text: 4.5.1 Sources of Heavy Metals in Solar Manufacturing

rows: Lead-based solder (if still used); residues from flux washes
Lead-free solder (Sn-Ag-Cu) – less toxic but still requires removal
Not used intentionally, but could appear in old electronic components or as impurity in raw materials
Possibly in old measuring instruments (thermometers, manometers) if not replaced
Contaminant in some chemicals or groundwater
Possible in anti-corrosion treatments for cooling water
Hexavalent chromium is carcinogenic; trivalent chromium is less toxic

body.text: 4.5.2 Source Segregation (Most Important Step)
The most effective way to reduce heavy metal discharge is to prevent mixing of heavy metal-laden streams with other wastewater.

rows: Soldering flux washing effluent (contains tin, lead, or other metals)
Collect in a separate tank; treat separately before mixing with general effluent.
Replace chromate inhibitors with non-toxic alternatives. If still present, segregate.
Handle as hazardous waste; never wash or throw into drains.

body.text: 4.5.3 Treatment Technologies
Depending on the concentration and volume, one or more of the following technologies shall be deployed:

rows: Adding hydroxide or sulphide to convert soluble heavy metal ions into insoluble precipitates (e.g., Pb(OH)₂, Cd(OH)₂). Solids are settled and removed as sludge.
For medium-to-high concentration streams (e.g., spent flux baths).
Using resin beads that exchange heavy metal cations (Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺, etc.) for harmless ions (H⁺, Na⁺). Resin is regenerated periodically, producing a small volume of concentrated metal solution.
Suitable for low-concentration, high-volume streams (e.g., rinses).
Activated carbon, zeolites, or bio-adsorbents capture heavy metals on their porous surface.
Final polishing after precipitation or ion exchange.
Membranes with very small pore sizes reject dissolved metal ions, producing pure water. Suitable for low-concentration streams but may be energy-intensive.
For producing high-purity reusable water and concentrating metals.
Alternating anion- and cation-exchange membranes under electric field separate ionic species. Useful for recovery of valuable metals.
Optional for high-value metal recovery (e.g., tin from solder rinse).

body.text: 4.5.4 Operational Procedure for Heavy Metal Removal

rows: Segregate heavy metal-containing streams at source using dedicated collection tanks or troughs. Label clearly with “WARNING: Contains Lead / Cadmium / etc.”
For chemical precipitation: Adjust pH to optimal value (refer to chemical manufacturer’s guidelines; e.g., for lead, pH ~9–10). Add precipitant (lime, caustic soda, sodium sulphide). Mix gently.
Allow floc to settle (or use a clarifier). Decant supernatant water to the next treatment stage (or to polishing).
Filter the settled sludge through a filter press or centrifuge to dewater. The solid cake is hazardous waste and must be stored in labelled drums and sent to a CHWTSDF.

For ion exchange: Pump the clarified wastewater through a column of cation-exchange resin. Monitor effluent periodically for metal breakthrough (using test kits or online analyser). Regenerate resin with acid when exhausted.
Final polishing with activated carbon or UF membrane to ensure discharge meets CPCB norms.
Record all treatment parameters in GS-WM-F25 – Heavy Metal Treatment Log.

body.text: 4.5.5 Monitoring of Heavy Metals
4.5.6 Sludge Management

Heavy metal-bearing sludge must be treated as hazardous waste (Category A210 as per Hazardous Waste Rules).
Store sludge in covered, labelled containers (UN-approved).
Transport only through authorised hazardous waste carriers.
Dispose at a CHWTSDF with appropriate incineration or stabilisation/solidification.
Obtain disposal certificates (Form 11) and retain for 5 years.
4.5.7 Source Reduction (Long-Term)

Replace lead-based solder with lead-free alternatives (Sn-Ag-Cu).
Switch to no-clean fluxes that reduce water washing requirements.
Replace chromate corrosion inhibitors in cooling towers with phosphate-based or non-toxic organic inhibitors.
Phase out mercury-containing equipment (thermometers, pressure gauges, fluorescent lamps) – see Section 4.8 of GS-EN-002.

blocks.text: 4.1 Collaboration with External Parties

body.text: Effective management of end-of-life solar modules and electrical equipment requires a multi-stakeholder approach. As India's installed solar capacity is projected to generate over 11 million tonnes of solar waste by 2047, no single company can build all the necessary collection, dismantling, and recycling infrastructure alone. Collaborations enable:

Economies of scale in reverse logistics
Access to specialised recycling technologies
Compliance with Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) obligations under the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022
Standardisation of waste handling across the industry

Gautam Solar shall actively participate in SolaREcycle India, the country's first solar-specific Producer Responsibility Organization, launched by the National Solar Energy Federation of India (NSEFI). Through this PRO, Gautam Solar will collaborate with other manufacturers, recyclers, technology providers, and developers to:

Establish common collection networks across states
Share best practices on dismantling and recycling
Work with the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) on policy development
Aggregate waste volumes to make recycling economically viable
Gautam Solar shall collaborate with research groups to advance solar waste management:

rows: Joint research on recycling technologies and development of domestic recycling capacity (similar to Attero's MoU with NISE).
Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW)
Data sharing and policy advocacy for circular economy in solar panels.
Participation in government-led R&D programmes for recycling and second-life applications of solar modules.

body.text: Gautam Solar shall be an active member of the Solar Waste Management Coalition under the Indian Solar Manufacturers Association (ISMA), working to:

Develop voluntary industry standards for collection and recycling
Create a shared reverse logistics platform
Engage with the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) on regulatory updates

Gautam Solar shall empanel and maintain a list of authorised e-waste recyclers and dismantlers (registered under the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022) for the handling of returned solar waste. Priority will be given to recyclers with high resource recovery rates (e.g., >95% recovery) and those that have achieved certifications such as R2 (Responsible Recycling) or e-Stewards. All recyclers must be listed on the CPCB's EPR Portal.

Gautam Solar shall work with state-level government agencies (e.g., State Pollution Control Boards, municipal corporations) to integrate its take-back scheme with existing e-waste collection centres, particularly in the states where it has major customer bases (Uttarakhand, Haryana, Delhi NCR). This will be done in a manner consistent with the CPCB's draft guidelines for solar waste.

steps.heading: 4.2.2 Information on Collection, Recycling and Disposal Infrastructure

body.text: The end-of-life information shall explicitly describe the available infrastructure to ensure that users can return modules free of charge (for residential and small commercial systems) or at low cost (for large utilities). The information includes:

Drop-off collection points at authorised dealer locations (list provided on the website)
Pick-up service for bulk volumes (≥10 modules) – users contact the helpline to schedule a free pick-up
Authorised recyclers – a list of CPCB-authorised recyclers to whom collected waste will be sent, including their contact details and recycling capabilities (e.g., recovery of glass, aluminium, copper, silver, silicon)
Prohibition of landfill – clear warnings that solar modules must never be disposed of in open areas or landfills, as they contain hazardous materials such as lead, cadmium, and antimony. The information explains that improper disposal can lead to soil and water contamination and poses health risks to communities and workers handling the waste.
The end-of-life information shall emphasise that returning modules for recycling contributes to:

Minimising waste to landfill – diverting thousands of tonnes of waste
Preventing leakage of hazardous substances into the environment
Reducing virgin material use – recycling aluminium, glass, copper, and silver from old modules can supply a significant portion of the materials needed for new modules. By 2047, recycling could meet approximately 60% of India's silicon demand and 50% of its aluminium demand.

All end-of-life information materials may include the Gautam Solar brand name and product trademarks (e.g., "G2X", "G2X N-type TOPCon", "R-Series") to ensure clear identification of the products covered.

steps.heading: 4.3 Reduction of Substances of Concern in Electrical and Electronic Equipment

body.text: The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 (and the 2023 amendment) aim to reduce the use of hazardous substances such as lead, mercury, and cadmium in the manufacture of electrical and electronic equipment. Rule 16 specifies a maximum concentration value (MCV) of 0.1% by weight for lead, mercury, hexavalent chromium, PBB, and PBDE in homogenous materials, and 0.01% for cadmium.

However, the 2023 amendment added two exemptions to Schedule II of the rules, including cadmium and lead in solar panels/cells, solar photovoltaic panels/cells/modules. These exemptions acknowledge the technical difficulties in immediately replacing lead in solders and cadmium in certain thin-film technologies. Nevertheless, Gautam Solar commits to voluntarily phasing out these substances wherever technically feasible.

Supplier declaration: All suppliers of materials (cells, ribbons, backsheets, cables) must complete a Restricted Substances Declaration form (GS-CE-F01), confirming compliance with Gautam Solar's RSL and the E-Waste Rules, 2022.

steps.heading: 4.4 Component Labelling for Collection and Sorting

body.text: Importance of Labelling. Solar modules contain a diverse mix of materials: glass (≈70% by weight), aluminium frames (≈15%), encapsulation polymers (≈5–8%), cells (≈3–5%, containing silicon, silver, copper, and trace metals), junction boxes (≈2%, containing plastics, copper, diodes), and cables (≈2%). Clear labelling enables downstream recyclers to sort components efficiently, maximising material recovery.
Label Specifications. Gautam Solar shall implement the following labelling practices:

Aluminium frame: Engraved or printed label with the material code Al and the recycling symbol (♻️) with number 40 (aluminium).
Junction box: Moulded-in symbol indicating PP (polypropylene) and PB FREE (lead-free solder) or HALOGEN-FREE as applicable.
Cable insulation: Periodic printing along the cable indicating XLPE (cross-linked polyethylene) or TPE (thermoplastic elastomer) and FREE OF PHTHALATES.
Glass: Permanent marking on the edge of the glass (laser-etched) indicating GLASS – RECYCLABLE and the thickness (e.g., 3.2mm).
Backsheet: Printed code indicating the type (e.g., PET or PVDF) and HALOGEN-FREE if applicable.

For modules that contain restricted substances above the threshold but within the regulatory exemption (e.g., lead-containing solder in older product lines), a visible label shall state: "CONTAINS LEAD – NOT FOR LANDFILL – RETURN TO GAUTAM SOLAR FOR RECYCLING"
Digital Labelling (QR Code). Every Gautam Solar module shall have a permanent QR code (laser-etched on the junction box or printed on the backsheet) that encodes:

Product model number
Manufacturing date
Material composition (glass, aluminium, polymer, cell type)
Location of hazardous substances (e.g., solder joints contain lead if pre-2027)
End-of-life handling instructions
Recyclers can scan the QR code at the time of decommissioning to instantly access detailed material data, facilitating automated sorting.

Identification of Hazardous Components. Components that contain restricted substances (e.g., soldered interconnections, diodes) shall be physically located and marked (via a diagram in the user manual and on the product label) to enable safe removal before shredding.

steps.heading: 4.5 Design for Circularity (Collection, Disassembly, Sorting, Remanufacturing, Recycling)

body.text: Guiding Principles. Gautam Solar adopts the following design principles to facilitate end-of-life circularity:

rows: Break down the product into independent, replaceable modules.
Junction box, frame, and connector are designed as separate, replaceable modules.
Use industry-standard connectors (e.g., Stäubli MC4-EVO2 equivalents) and frame profiles to maximise interoperability and repairability.
All junction boxes use standard MC4-compatible connectors. Frame dimensions follow the industry standard for 60-cell and 72-cell formats.
Avoid permanent adhesives or welds where disassembly is required. Use screws, clips, or snap-fits.
Frame is attached using mechanical clamps, not glued to the backsheet. Junction box is secured with clips and sealant (but sealant is peelable).
Avoid composites that cannot be separated (e.g., metal-polymer laminates). Use mono-material components where possible.
Frame is pure aluminium; junction box body is pure polypropylene; cable is XLPE.
Incorporate post-consumer recycled (PCR) materials, such as recycled aluminium for frames and recycled glass for new glass.
Target: 30% recycled aluminium in frames by 2028.

body.text: Design for Disassembly (DfD). Gautam Solar's modules are designed to be disassembled using common hand tools without damaging reusable components. The disassembly steps are:

rows: Cut off cables from junction box

body.text: A disassembly manual (GS-CE-F02) is available on the company website for use by recyclers.

Remanufacturing. Modules that are returned under the take-back scheme and are still functional (e.g., after minor cell failure but overall >80% of original output) shall be routed to a remanufacturing line at the Haridwar factory. Remanufacturing includes:

Replacing failed bypass diodes
Repairing minor junction box damage
Re-framing if required
Retesting (EL, IV, insulation) to certify output and safety

Remanufactured modules are sold with a limited 5-year warranty as "Certified Pre-owned" for applications where absolute long-term reliability is not required (e.g., off-grid systems, temporary installations).
Recycling of Non-Remanufacturable Modules. Modules that cannot be remanufactured are sent to authorised recyclers who recover materials using processes such as:

Mechanical recycling: Glass crushing, metal separation, polymer pyrolysis
Thermal delamination: Removing the encapsulant (EVA/POE) to free silicon cells
Chemical leaching: Recovering silver and copper from cells
Gautam Solar requires recyclers to achieve material recovery rates of at least 90% for glass and aluminium, and >95% for silver and copper, wherever technically feasible.

steps.heading: 4.6 Collection Scheme – Free Return and Buy-Back

body.text: Overview of Collection Scheme. Gautam Solar implements a national take-back scheme that allows any consumer (residential, commercial, or industrial) to return end-of-life Gautam Solar modules free of charge (for residential and small commercial systems) or at a low, negotiated cost (for large utility volumes). The scheme complies with the CPCB's mandate for producers to establish collection mechanisms and publicise take-back systems.
Return Methods.
